text:
MUSOKO — AI-Powered Local Food Marketplace
Application Design and Development Prompt (v5)
Build the first version now. Do not stop after generating a design description or project plan.
Sections 1–3 define what to build and how it will be judged. They take priority over everything else.
Sections 4–11 describe how to build it. Section 12 describes later phases and is context only.

1. Build This Now (Phase 1 scope)
Build Musoko, a responsive web application that helps households and other buyers discover local
farmers and their products in the Arkansas Delta, and contact those farmers directly.
Deliver a working, interactive application, not static mockups, containing exactly these parts:
    1. Musoko design system (colors, type, reusable components).
    2. Homepage and responsive navigation.
    3. Product marketplace with search, sorting, filtering, and unit-price comparison.
    4. Farmer directory.
    5. Farmer profile page.
    6. Interactive map of farms, farmers markets, and pickup locations.
    7. Farmers market list page (basic: name, town, days and hours, participating farmers).
    8. Buyer inquiry flow, including the farmer's reply back to the buyer.
    9. Farmer registration.
    10. Farmer dashboard: profile, products and availability, inquiries and replies, optional outcome
        follow-up, basic engagement numbers.
    11. Basic administrator dashboard: review farmer registrations, create and manage a profile on a
        farmer's behalf, hide or remove listings, verify individual claims, and view pilot metrics.
    12. Anonymous logging of searches and inquiries by product and community (Section 9), so local
        supply and demand can be analysed later.
The buyer experience comes first. A household buyer opening Musoko should be able to answer three
questions within seconds, and every buyer-facing screen should be judged against them:
    •   What fresh food is available near me?
    •   How much does it cost?
    •   Where and when can I get it?
Do not build in this version: the AI business assistant, the institutional buyer portal, purchasing requests
and quotes, food-access program discovery, in-app checkout, payment processing, commissions, or any
Musoko-operated delivery. Design the data model and navigation so these can be added later (see
Section 12), but ship no partial or placeholder versions of them beyond a short "coming soon" mention
on the homepage.

Definition of done
    •   The application installs and runs end-to-end with no external credentials, using seeded
        demonstration data (Section 10) in a demo mode.
    •   Real services (database, authentication, map tiles, notifications) sit behind a clear integration
        interface and are switched on by environment variables.
    •   A README gives setup steps and lists exactly what remains to be configured for production.
    •   Every acceptance criterion in Section 3 passes.

2. Hard Constraints
Transaction model. Musoko facilitates discovery and direct buyer–farmer connection only. Farmers and
buyers arrange payment and fulfillment themselves. Musoko is not a party to any transaction, and the
interface must say so wherever an inquiry is sent.
Demonstration data. All farms, farmers, products, prices, inventory, and market participation in this
version are fictional. Never present them as verified real-world information.
Location privacy. Never publicly reveal a private farm address or exact coordinates without the farmer's
explicit opt-in.
Contact privacy. Never show a farmer's phone number or email publicly unless the farmer opts in. By
default, buyers reach farmers through the inquiry form.
Claims. Do not imply that every farmer accepts SNAP/EBT, that any product qualifies for a healthcare or
nutrition benefit, or that prices are guaranteed affordable. Make prices and options easy to find and
compare instead.
Secrets. Never expose API keys or other secrets in frontend code.
Positioning. Musoko is a farmer-centered local food marketplace. It must not look or read like a grocery
delivery app: no cart, no checkout, no delivery-time promises.

3. Acceptance Criteria
Demo labelling
    •   A persistent banner on every page states that the site is showing demonstration data.
    •   Every fictional farm, product, and market carries a visible "Demo" badge on cards, profiles, and
        map previews.
Demo mode behaviour
    •   Changes made during a demo persist across page navigation, role switching, and page reload for
        the length of the session: farmer profile and listing edits, availability confirmations, new
        registrations, inquiries, replies, outcomes, and administrator actions.
    •   The roles share one data set. An inquiry sent as a buyer appears in that farmer's dashboard, the
        farmer's reply appears on the buyer's inquiry status page, and both appear in the administrator
        metrics.

•     A "Reset demo data" control restores the original seed data.
    •     No screen may appear to save a change that is then lost.
Privacy
    •     Public map pins for farms sit at the town centre (or a similarly coarse point) unless the farmer
          has opted in to showing the exact location.
    •     Exact coordinates and street addresses are stored in a separate table from public location data
          and are never returned by any public query or API response.
    •     A farmer's phone and email appear publicly only when the farmer has switched that on.
Availability status
    •     Every product listing shows exactly one of three statuses and a "last updated" date:
 Status                            Meaning
 Available now                     The farmer confirmed availability within the last 14 days (configurable).
 Coming soon                       The farmer expects the product in a future season, and has given an
                                   expected month.
 Availability unconfirmed          The listing has not been confirmed recently.

•     "Available now" listings rank first by default. "Availability unconfirmed" listings rank last. A
          listing moves from "Available now" to "Availability unconfirmed" automatically when the
          confirmation window lapses.
    •     The farmer dashboard offers a one-tap "still available" confirmation for each listing, and a
          simple way to set a product to "Coming soon."
Quantity
    •     Availability status and quantity are separate. A listing may optionally state the quantity on hand,
          with its unit and its own last-confirmed date, for example "About 20 lb available · confirmed Nov
          12."
    •     Nothing about quantity is shown when the farmer has not entered it. An "Available now" listing
          with no quantity is valid.
    •     Quantity is shown as the farmer's estimate, never as guaranteed or reserved stock. Sending an
          inquiry does not reduce it.
    •     When confirming "still available," the farmer can update the quantity in the same step.
    •     When a buyer's requested quantity exceeds the stated quantity, the inquiry form says so and
          still allows the inquiry to be sent.
Assisted onboarding and consent
    •     A profile created by an administrator is a draft and is not publicly visible until the farmer's
          consent to publish is recorded.
    •     Consent is recorded either by the farmer approving the profile after signing in, or by the
          administrator logging how it was given (in person, by phone, or on a signed form), the date, and
          who recorded it.

•   When an administrator later changes public information on a farmer's behalf, the profile is
        marked "awaiting farmer review" in the administrator dashboard until the farmer's review is
        recorded the same way.
    •   A farmer can unpublish their own profile at any time.
Price comparison
    •   When a listing includes a measurable size (weight, volume, or count), the card shows a
        normalized unit price alongside the listed price, for example "$15 for a 5 lb box · $3.00 per lb."
    •   Sorting by price uses the normalized unit price within the same product type.
    •   No conversion is shown when it would be unreliable (for example a bunch, a basket, or "each"
        with no stated weight). Those listings show the listed price and unit only.
Inquiries and replies
    •   A buyer can send an inquiry from a product card or a farmer profile in three steps or fewer, and
        chooses how they want to be answered (text or email).
    •   The inquiry is stored, appears in the farmer dashboard, and triggers a notification through the
        notification interface (logged to console in demo mode).
    •   The farmer can reply with one tap using "Available," "Sold out," or "Contact me," with an
        optional short message. The reply is delivered to the buyer by their chosen method through the
        notification interface.
    •   "Contact me" shares the farmer's phone number with that buyer only, and only after the farmer
        confirms. No other reply reveals the farmer's contact details.
    •   The buyer's contact details are visible only to the farmer they wrote to and to administrators.
    •   The inquiry form has basic abuse protection (rate limiting and a spam check).
    •   Every inquiry screen states that payment and pickup are arranged directly with the farmer.
Inquiry status and unanswered inquiries
    •   Every inquiry shows one of three statuses to the buyer, the farmer, and administrators:
        "Awaiting response," "Responded," or "Closed."
    •   The buyer's confirmation message includes a private link to a status page for that inquiry, since
        buyers have no account.
    •   If an inquiry is still awaiting a response after a configurable period (default 48 hours), the farmer
        receives one reminder.
    •   An inquiry that stays unanswered for a further configurable period (default 14 days) closes
        automatically. The buyer is told, and is pointed to other "Available now" listings of the same
        product type.
    •   A responded inquiry closes once the farmer records an outcome, or automatically after the
        same period.
    •   Musoko never promises a response or a response time. Confirmation wording says the farmer
        will reply when they can.
Trust labels
    •   "Listed" means only that Musoko reviewed the profile for publication. Approving a registration
        never produces a "Verified" label.

•   "Verified" attaches to a single claim (for example, a specific certification), never to a farmer or
       farm as a whole, and appears only when an administrator has recorded what evidence was
       checked and when.
   •   Every other claim, including SNAP/EBT acceptance, growing practices, licences, and
       certifications, appears only when the farmer has entered it and is labelled "farmer-reported."
Outcome follow-up
   •   Some days after an inquiry is answered, the farmer dashboard asks, optionally: "Did this inquiry
       result in a sale or new customer relationship?" with the answers "Yes, a sale," "Yes, a new
       potential customer," "No," and "Still discussing."
   •   No sale amount or payment detail is requested. Skipping the question has no consequence for
       the farmer.
Local supply and demand data
   •   Each search is logged with its terms, filters, selected community, and number of results, with no
       name, contact detail, or account attached.
   •   Searches that return no results are recorded and visible to administrators.
   •   Each inquiry records the pickup location, farmers market, or farmer-managed delivery option
       the buyer chose.
   •   Opens of pickup location and farmers market previews, on the map and in lists, are counted in
       aggregate by location, with nothing tied to an individual.
Data privacy
   •   Leaving out names and accounts is not treated as sufficient for anonymity. Detailed searches in
       a small community can still point to an individual.
   •   Data minimization: search events store no IP address, device identifier, or precise location, only
       the selected community. The time is stored to the day, not the minute. Search text is kept short,
       and anything resembling a phone number, email address, or street address is stripped before
       storage.
   •   Retention: raw search events are reduced to aggregate counts and deleted after a configurable
       period. Buyer contact details are deleted a configurable period after the inquiry closes, leaving
       the product type, community, status, and outcome for analysis.
   •   Small samples: community-level figures are not displayed when they rest on fewer than a
       configurable minimum number of farms, searches, or inquiries. The dashboard shows "not
       enough data" instead. This applies to every analytics view, including outcomes and SNAP/EBT
       counts.
   •   Raw search events and individual inquiries are visible only to administrators, never to farmers or
       the public.
Accessibility and performance
   •   Keyboard navigable, sufficient color contrast, labelled form fields, alt text on images.
   •   The product list view, not the map, is the default on phones. The map loads only when the user
       opens it.
   •   Images are compressed and lazy-loaded. Target an initial mobile page load under roughly 1 MB.

•   Plain language throughout, large touch targets, and no step that requires typing when a choice
        will do.

4. Project Context
Tagline: Connecting Local Farmers and Communities.
Musoko is an initiative developed by ReMix Ideas, initially serving the Arkansas Delta, with the potential
to expand to other regions.
It addresses two connected problems:
    1. Small farmers often struggle to find reliable markets, access business intelligence, and build
       profitable enterprises.
    2. Many communities struggle to access affordable, fresh, nutritious, locally grown food.
Core vision: a thriving local food economy where small farmers have greater economic opportunity and
communities have better access to affordable, nutritious food.
How success will be measured in the pilot (the dashboards should make these visible):
    •   Inquiries sent.
    •   Inquiries answered, and how quickly.
    •   Inquiries that closed without a response.
    •   Farmer-reported outcomes: sales and new customer relationships resulting from inquiries.
    •   Listings confirmed in the last 14 days.
    •   Active farmers by community.
    •   Number of farmers reporting SNAP/EBT acceptance, labelled as self-reported.
    •   Most-inquired products by community, and searches that returned no results.
    •   Most-chosen pickup locations and farmers markets.
Outcome and SNAP/EBT figures are self-reported and must be labelled that way wherever they are
shown. Community-level figures based on too few farmers, searches, or inquiries are withheld, as set
out under "Data privacy" in Section 3.
Longer-term direction. Musoko is not meant to remain a farmer directory. ReMix Ideas intends to build
its own AI-powered platform on hyperlocal information. The first version must therefore capture data in
a form that can later answer questions such as:
    •   What products are farmers offering in a particular community?
    •   Where are buyers searching for products that are not currently listed?
    •   Which products receive the most inquiries?
    •   Where are the gaps between local supply and expressed buyer interest?
    •   What opportunities might exist for farmers to coordinate production?
    •   Which pickup locations and farmers markets do buyers choose most, and which communities
        have buyer interest but no convenient pickup point?

Food-access intelligence. This is where the pilot contributes most to Musoko's longer-term
development. Over time, aggregated information should show which products households are looking
for, where local supply falls short, and which pickup locations are most useful. That serves two
audiences: farmers, who can make better production and marketing decisions, and the organizations
shaping food-access strategy in the region.
Phase 1 collects and structures this data and shows simple counts to administrators. It does not build
analysis, forecasting, or recommendations. Wherever these counts appear, state that they reflect only
people who used Musoko, not the whole community, and that early pilot numbers are small.

5. Design Direction
The platform should feel welcoming, trustworthy, modern, and rooted in agriculture. The visual identity
should reflect the relationship between soil, farmers, food, families, and communities.
    •   Clean, contemporary, mobile-first interface.
    •   Deep forest green, warm earth tones, cream, and restrained harvest-gold accents.
    •   Generous whitespace, readable typography, intuitive navigation.
    •   Authentic agricultural imagery of small farmers, fresh produce, and local communities. Use
        placeholders or openly licensed images in the demo, never photos of identifiable real farmers
        presented as demo profiles.
    •   Usable by people with varying levels of digital literacy and on slow rural connections.
    •   Clear calls to action without unnecessary complexity.

6. Users in This Version
Farmers and local producers can:
    •   Register and create a farm profile, or have an administrator create one for them.
    •   Describe their farm, practices, and products, and add photographs.
    •   List products with price, unit, quantity, and seasonal availability.
    •   Choose pickup locations and schedules, and say whether they offer their own delivery.
    •   Link their profile to the farmers markets where they sell.
    •   Receive buyer inquiries and reply with one tap.
    •   Optionally report whether an inquiry led to a sale or a new customer.
    •   Control whether their exact location and their contact details are public.
    •   Optionally note whether they are open to wholesale or institutional supply (a simple flag for
        now).
Households and other buyers can:
    •   Search by product, location, price, and availability.
    •   Browse the map of farms, markets, and pickup locations.
    •   View and compare products.

•   Send an inquiry to a farmer.
    •   See pickup options and farmer-managed delivery where offered.
Administrators can:
    •   Review and approve farmer registrations.
    •   Create and manage profiles and listings on a farmer's behalf (assisted onboarding), publishing
        only once the farmer's consent is recorded.
    •   Hide or remove listings and markets.
    •   Mark an individual claim as verified, recording the evidence checked.
    •   See the pilot metrics in Section 4.
Buyers do not need an account to browse or to send an inquiry in this version. An inquiry asks only for
name, a way to be reached, and a message.

7. Feature Specifications
A. Homepage
    •   Musoko logo and tagline.
    •   Prominent search bar: "What local food are you looking for?"
    •   Location selector, initially limited to Arkansas Delta communities.
    •   One dominant action: "Find Local Food." "Explore Farmers" and "Join as a Farmer" are present
        but visually secondary.
    •   Food that is available now near the selected community, with price and pickup details visible
        without opening a listing.
    •   Featured farmers and nearby farmers markets, below the available food.
    •   "How Musoko works" section, including that buyers and farmers arrange payment and pickup
        directly.
    •   A short section on affordable, nutritious food, worded per the claims constraint.
    •   A brief "coming soon" note for AI tools for farmers and institutional buying.

B. Product Marketplace
Categories: fresh vegetables, fresh fruits, herbs, eggs, meat and poultry, dairy, grains and legumes, other
locally produced foods.
Product cards show photo, farmer name, town, listed price and unit, normalized unit price where
reliable, availability status, where and when it can be picked up, last-updated date, and the Demo
badge.
Each product is assigned a standard product type from a shared list (for example "tomatoes," "collard
greens," "eggs") in addition to the farmer's own title, so the same food can be compared across farms
and counted across communities.

The listing form captures price, the selling unit, and, where it applies, the size of that unit as a number
and a measure (for example 5 lb, 1 dozen, 1 pint). The form should make this easy with common presets
rather than free text.
The form also offers an optional "about how much do you have?" field, in the same selling unit. It is
clearly optional and can be left blank.
Filters: category, product type, town or distance, price range, availability status, pickup or farmer-
managed delivery, farmer-reported SNAP/EBT acceptance. Sorting: unit price, distance, recently
updated. "Available now" is the default view.
For meat, poultry, dairy, and eggs, the listing form asks the farmer to confirm they hold whatever licence
or inspection applies to them, and the listing shows "farmer-reported" beside it. Musoko does not verify
this.

C. Farmer Directory and Profiles
Each profile includes:
    •   Farm or business name, farmer introduction and story.
    •   General location (town or county).
    •   Photographs.
    •   Products, seasonal availability, prices, and units.
    •   Pickup and delivery information, and markets attended.
    •   Inquiry button.
    •   Growing practices, licences, and certifications, where the farmer chooses to share them, each
        labelled "farmer-reported" or, for a claim an administrator has checked against evidence,
        "verified" with the date.
    •   Optional flag: open to wholesale or institutional supply.
A published profile is "Listed." Do not display a general "Verified farmer" or "Verified farm" badge
anywhere.

D. Interactive Map
Displays participating farms (coarse location by default), farmers markets, and public pickup locations,
with the products linked to each.
Filters: product category, distance, availability, pickup or farmer-managed delivery, farmers markets
only.
Selecting a marker opens a preview with a link to the full profile or market entry. Provide an equivalent
list view for users who cannot or prefer not to use the map.

E. Farmers Market List
Market name, town, operating days and hours, participating farmers, commonly offered products,
directions link, and market contact information.

F. Buyer Inquiry Flow
    1. Buyer selects "Contact farmer" on a product or profile.

2. Buyer enters name, how they want to be answered (text or email), the product and rough
       quantity if relevant, a pickup location or delivery option chosen from those the farmer offers,
       and a message.
    3. Confirmation screen explains next steps and that Musoko is not a party to the sale.
    4. The farmer is notified and replies with one tap: "Available," "Sold out," or "Contact me," with an
       optional short message.
    5. The buyer receives the reply by their chosen method.
This is a single inquiry and reply, not a chat thread. Keep it that simple in this version.
The farmer is notified through a notification interface designed for SMS and email. In demo mode it logs
the message. The README must state that an SMS provider is to be configured for production, since
many farmers will rely on text messages.

G. Farmer Registration and Dashboard
Registration is short and can be completed on a phone. Support phone-number sign-in as well as email
in the authentication interface (simulated in demo mode with a role switcher).
Dashboard sections: profile, products and availability (with one-tap "still available" and "coming soon"),
inquiries (awaiting response, responded, closed, with the optional outcome question), privacy settings,
and basic numbers (profile views, inquiries received, inquiries answered).

H. Administrator Dashboard
Registration review queue, create or edit on behalf of a farmer with consent and review status shown
for each profile, a list of inquiries awaiting response, listing and market moderation, claim verification
(claim, evidence checked, date, who checked it), and the pilot metrics, including most-inquired products
by community and searches with no results.

8. Technical Requirements
Build a responsive web application for phones, tablets, and desktops.
    •   Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript.
    •   Styling: Tailwind CSS with accessible UI components.
    •   Backend and database: Supabase with PostgreSQL, with PostGIS for distance queries.
    •   Authentication: role-based accounts (farmer, buyer, administrator), with phone and email sign-
        in.
    •   Mapping: MapLibre with an openly available tile source, so no token is needed to run the demo.
    •   Notifications: an interface for SMS and email, stubbed in demo mode.
    •   Hosting: any environment compatible with this stack.
Implement role-based access control, row-level security, input validation, image upload and storage
with compression, secure server-side API endpoints, and the privacy controls in Section 2.
Demo mode. A single environment switch runs the whole application on local seed data with simulated
sign-in and no external services. Demo data lives in one shared store that every screen reads from and
writes to, kept in the browser so it survives navigation and reload, with a reset control (see "Demo mode

behaviour" in Section 3). With the switch off, the same code uses Supabase, real authentication, and real
notifications.
If the build environment cannot run this stack (for example, a single-page preview tool), build the same
scope as a self-contained interactive application on the seed data, keep the same component structure
and data shapes, and say clearly what was substituted.

9. Data Architecture
Entities for this version:
    •   Regions (so Musoko can expand beyond the Arkansas Delta without restructuring).
    •   Users and roles.
    •   Farmer profiles, including who created the profile, publication status (draft, published,
        unpublished), consent to publish (method, date, recorded by), and whether the farmer has
        reviewed the latest changes made on their behalf.
    •   Farm public locations (town, county, coarse coordinates).
    •   Farm private locations (exact address and coordinates) — a separate table with its own access
        rules, because row-level security does not hide individual columns.
    •   Communities within a region (towns and counties), used consistently for farms, markets, pickup
        locations, searches, and inquiries.
    •   Product types: a shared, standard list that every product is mapped to.
    •   Products, with price, selling unit, unit size and measure, and a stored normalized unit price
        where one can be calculated.
    •   Product availability: status, last-confirmed date, expected month for "Coming soon," and a
        history of status changes over time.
    •   Product quantity (optional): amount, unit, and its own last-confirmed date, kept separate from
        availability status so it can support larger and institutional orders later.
    •   Farmers markets and farmer–market relationships.
    •   Pickup locations.
    •   Buyer inquiries, linked to product, product type, farmer, community, and chosen pickup location
        or delivery option, with status (awaiting response, responded, closed), requested quantity,
        reminder sent, reason for closing, and timestamps. Buyer contact details are held separately so
        they can be deleted on schedule without losing the rest.
    •   Inquiry replies and farmer-reported outcomes.
    •   Claims (SNAP/EBT acceptance, practices, licences, certifications), each with a status of farmer-
        reported or verified, and for verified claims the evidence checked, date, and administrator.
    •   Search events: shortened and cleaned terms, matched product type if any, filters, selected
        community, result count, and date. No personal identifiers, IP address, device identifier, or
        precise location.
    •   Aggregate counts by product type, community, pickup location, and period, which outlive the
        raw search events.

•    Settings for the configurable values: availability confirmation window, reminder and auto-close
         periods, retention periods, and minimum sample size for display.
Design these tables so the questions listed under "Longer-term direction" in Section 4 can be answered
with straightforward queries, without restructuring.
Reserve, but do not build screens for: buyer profiles, saved listings, institutional purchasing requests,
food-access programs, and AI assistant conversation history.

10. Seed Data
Create clearly fictional demonstration data:
    •    About 12 farms spread across Helena-West Helena, Pine Bluff, Forrest City, and surrounding
         Delta communities.
    •    About 40 products across all categories, with varied prices, units, and seasons, covering all three
         availability statuses.
    •    Several farms selling the same product type in different unit sizes (for example tomatoes by the
         pound and by the 5 lb box), plus a few listings where no unit conversion is possible.
    •    Mostly farmer-reported claims, with two or three verified claims so the difference is visible.
    •    Sample search events, including some with no results.
    •    Some listings with a stated quantity and some without, including one "Available now" listing
         with a small quantity.
    •    One administrator-created profile still in draft awaiting the farmer's consent, and one published
         profile marked "awaiting farmer review."
    •    At least one community with too little data, so the "not enough data" state is visible.
    •    5 farmers markets and 3 public pickup locations.
    •    A mix of privacy settings: some farms showing exact location, most not; some with public
         contact details, most not.
    •    A few farms with farmer-reported SNAP/EBT acceptance, most without.
    •    Sample inquiries in all three statuses, including one closed without a response and some with
         reported outcomes.
    •    One farmer, one buyer, and one administrator demo account.
Use invented farm and farmer names that do not match real businesses.

11. Build Sequence
Work in this order, keeping the application runnable after each step:
    1.   Project structure, design system, seed data, and demo mode.
    2.   Homepage and navigation.
    3.   Product marketplace, farmer directory, and farmer profile.
    4.   Map and farmers market list.

5.   Buyer inquiry flow.
    6.   Farmer registration and dashboard.
    7.   Administrator dashboard.
    8.   README, and a check of every acceptance criterion in Section 3.
Create reusable components and a maintainable project structure.

12. Later Phases (context only — do not build now)
Phase 2 — AI and institutional market access
AI farmer business assistant. A conversational assistant, accessible to farmers with limited technical
experience, that helps with product descriptions, marketing messages, costs and pricing, profit
estimates from farmer-provided data, business plans, customer segments, introductions to institutional
buyers, procurement requirements, seasonal opportunities, and collaboration to meet larger orders. It
must clearly separate verified platform data from estimates, assumptions, and general guidance, and
must not claim to know actual demand, prices, or purchasing requirements without reliable data.
Integrated server-side only.
Institutional buyer portal. Organization profiles for schools, universities, hospitals, restaurants, and food
service providers; supplier discovery; purchasing requests with specifications, quantities, and delivery or
pickup needs; requests for quotes; inquiry tracking; and a way for farmers to express interest. Requests
never become binding orders or contracts automatically. Farmer profiles will need fields institutional
buyers typically ask about, such as food-safety certification and insurance.
Buyer accounts and dashboard. Saved farmers and products, submitted inquiries, purchasing requests,
preferred pickup locations.
Basic market insights drawn from actual platform data.
Phase 3 — Food access and regional intelligence
    •    Discovery of participating food-access programs and their locations, on the map and in filters.
    •    Information on eligible Food Is Medicine and produce prescription programs and partnerships.
    •    Hyperlocal supply and demand analysis.
    •    AI-powered food-access intelligence built on the aggregated pilot data: which products
         households seek, where local supply is insufficient, and which pickup locations are most useful.
         Findings are shared back with farmers in plain language to guide what to grow and where to sell,
         and with food-access partners to inform where programs and pickup points are needed. The
         small-sample and privacy rules in Section 3 apply to everything shown, and findings are
         presented as signals from Musoko users, not as measured community demand.
    •    Advanced AI recommendations.
    •    Farmer collaboration and aggregation.
    •    Fuller administrator tools: buyer and institutional account management, food-access program
         information, geographic participation data, content and safety management.

13. Brand Identity
Name: MUSOKO
Tagline: Connecting Local Farmers and Communities.
Personality: rooted, welcoming, innovative, trustworthy, community-centered, forward-looking.
Story: Musoko combines "Mu," from Mutalemwa, and "Soko," the Swahili word for market. The name
stands for a marketplace where farmers, buyers, and communities connect to create economic
opportunity and improve access to nutritious food.
Use Musoko as the public-facing brand. ReMix Ideas may appear in the About section or legal footer as
the organization developing the platform.
The logo and visual identity should be original, simple, and adaptable to mobile apps, websites, signage,
and print.

14. Open Items for the Project Owner (not for the builder)
    •   Check "Musoko" for trademark and domain conflicts before investing in the logo.
    •   Have someone familiar with Arkansas rules confirm what applies to selling meat, poultry, dairy,
        eggs, and prepared foods, and adjust the listing form wording.
    •   Draft terms of use and a privacy notice, including the statement that Musoko is not a party to
        transactions.
    •   Choose an SMS provider and decide who pays for messages.
    •   Decide who will onboard the first farmers and keep listings fresh during the pilot.
    •   Decide what evidence is required before a claim can be marked verified, and who is allowed to
        do it.
    •   Set a data policy: who owns the search, inquiry, and outcome data, how farmers are told it is
        collected, and how community-level findings will be shared back with them.
    •   Set the actual values for the retention periods and the minimum sample size for showing
        community-level figures. The prompt leaves these configurable.
    •   Decide what form of farmer consent Musoko will accept for publishing a profile created on a
        farmer's behalf.

The goal is not simply another food marketplace. It is digital infrastructure that helps local farmers
thrive economically while making fresh, nutritious food more accessible and affordable for the
communities around them.

# ACCEPTANCE.md

# Acceptance criteria

Section 3 of the brief, numbered so each one can be traced to a test and reported on. Wording follows the brief. Where a line here and the brief differ, the brief is right.

Mark each line in the step report as pass, fail or not yet built. Never mark a line pass without having exercised it in the running app or in a test.

## Definition of done (Section 1)

- **DONE-1** Installs and runs end to end with no external credentials, on seeded demonstration data, in demo mode.
- **DONE-2** Real services (database, authentication, map tiles, notifications) sit behind a clear integration interface and are switched on by environment variables.
- **DONE-3** A README gives setup steps and lists exactly what remains to be configured for production, including that an SMS provider must be configured.
- **DONE-4** Every criterion below passes.

## Scope (Section 1)

- **SCOPE-1** All twelve parts exist and are interactive: design system, homepage and navigation, marketplace, farmer directory, farmer profile, map, farmers market list, inquiry flow with reply, farmer registration, farmer dashboard, administrator dashboard, anonymous logging.
- **SCOPE-2** None of these exist beyond one short "coming soon" mention on the homepage: AI assistant, institutional portal, purchasing requests and quotes, food-access program discovery, checkout, payments, commissions, Musoko-run delivery.
- **SCOPE-3** Nothing looks or reads like a grocery delivery app: no cart, no checkout, no delivery-time promises.

## Demo labelling

- **DEMO-1** A persistent banner on every page states that the site is showing demonstration data. (Met by the demo strip. The watermark is additional.)
- **DEMO-2** Every fictional farm, product and market carries a visible "Demo" badge on cards, profiles and map previews.

## Demo mode behaviour

- **MODE-1** Changes persist across navigation, role switching and reload: profile and listing edits, availability confirmations, new registrations, inquiries, replies, outcomes, administrator actions.
- **MODE-2** Roles share one data set. A buyer's inquiry appears in that farmer's dashboard, the farmer's reply appears on the buyer's status page, and both appear in administrator metrics.
- **MODE-3** "Reset demo data" restores the original seed.
- **MODE-4** No screen appears to save a change that is then lost.

## Privacy

- **PRIV-1** Public farm pins sit at the town centre or a similarly coarse point unless the farmer opted in to the exact location.
- **PRIV-2** Exact coordinates and street addresses are stored in a separate table and are never returned by any public query or API response.
- **PRIV-3** A farmer's phone and email appear publicly only when the farmer switched that on.

## Availability status

- **AVAIL-1** Every listing shows exactly one of "Available now", "Coming soon", "Availability unconfirmed", and a "last updated" date.
- **AVAIL-2** "Available now" means confirmed within the last 14 days, configurable. "Coming soon" carries an expected month.
- **AVAIL-3** "Available now" ranks first by default and "Availability unconfirmed" ranks last.
- **AVAIL-4** A listing moves from "Available now" to "Availability unconfirmed" automatically when the window lapses.
- **AVAIL-5** The farmer dashboard has a one-tap "still available" for each listing and a simple way to set "Coming soon".

## Quantity

- **QTY-1** Status and quantity are separate. A listing may state quantity with its unit and its own last-confirmed date, for example "About 20 lb available · confirmed Nov 12".
- **QTY-2** Nothing about quantity is shown when the farmer has not entered it. "Available now" with no quantity is valid.
- **QTY-3** Quantity is shown as the farmer's estimate, never as guaranteed or reserved. Sending an inquiry does not reduce it.
- **QTY-4** When confirming "still available" the farmer can update the quantity in the same step.
- **QTY-5** When the requested quantity exceeds the stated quantity, the inquiry form says so and still allows sending.

## Assisted onboarding and consent

- **CONS-1** A profile created by an administrator is a draft and is not publicly visible until consent to publish is recorded.
- **CONS-2** Consent is recorded either by the farmer approving after signing in, or by the administrator logging the method (in person, by phone, signed form), the date and who recorded it.
- **CONS-3** When an administrator later changes public information, the profile is marked "awaiting farmer review" in the administrator dashboard until the farmer's review is recorded the same way.
- **CONS-4** A farmer can unpublish their own profile at any time.

## Price comparison

- **PRICE-1** When a listing has a measurable size, the card shows a normalized unit price beside the listed price, for example "$15 for a 5 lb box · $3.00 per lb".
- **PRICE-2** Sorting by price uses the normalized unit price within the same product type.
- **PRICE-3** No conversion is shown when it would be unreliable (bunch, basket, "each" with no weight). Those show listed price and unit only.

## Inquiries and replies

- **INQ-1** A buyer can send an inquiry from a product card or a farmer profile in three steps or fewer, and chooses text or email for the answer.
- **INQ-2** The inquiry is stored, appears in the farmer dashboard, and triggers a notification through the notification interface (console in demo mode).
- **INQ-3** The farmer replies with one tap: "Available", "Sold out" or "Contact me", with an optional short message. The reply goes to the buyer by their chosen method through the notification interface.
- **INQ-4** "Contact me" shares the farmer's phone with that buyer only, and only after the farmer confirms. No other reply reveals contact details.
- **INQ-5** The buyer's contact details are visible only to the farmer they wrote to and to administrators.
- **INQ-6** The inquiry form has basic abuse protection: rate limiting and a spam check.
- **INQ-7** Every inquiry screen states that payment and pickup are arranged directly with the farmer.

## Inquiry status and unanswered inquiries

- **STAT-1** Every inquiry shows "Awaiting response", "Responded" or "Closed" to the buyer, the farmer and administrators.
- **STAT-2** The buyer's confirmation includes a private link to a status page for that inquiry.
- **STAT-3** After a configurable period, default 48 hours, an unanswered inquiry sends the farmer one reminder.
- **STAT-4** After a further configurable period, default 14 days, an unanswered inquiry closes automatically. The buyer is told and is pointed to other "Available now" listings of the same product type.
- **STAT-5** A responded inquiry closes when the farmer records an outcome, or automatically after the same period.
- **STAT-6** Musoko never promises a response or a response time. Confirmation wording says the farmer will reply when they can.

## Trust labels

- **TRUST-1** "Listed" means only that Musoko reviewed the profile for publication. Approving a registration never produces a "Verified" label.
- **TRUST-2** "Verified" attaches to a single claim, never to a farmer or farm, and appears only when an administrator has recorded what evidence was checked and when.
- **TRUST-3** Every other claim (SNAP/EBT, practices, licences, certifications) appears only when the farmer entered it and is labelled "farmer-reported".
- **TRUST-4** No "Verified farmer" or "Verified farm" badge exists anywhere.

## Outcome follow-up

- **OUT-1** Some days after an inquiry is answered, the farmer dashboard optionally asks "Did this inquiry result in a sale or new customer relationship?" with "Yes, a sale", "Yes, a new potential customer", "No", "Still discussing".
- **OUT-2** No sale amount or payment detail is requested. Skipping has no consequence.

## Local supply and demand data

- **DATA-1** Each search is logged with terms, filters, selected community and result count, with no name, contact detail or account.
- **DATA-2** Searches with no results are recorded and visible to administrators.
- **DATA-3** Each inquiry records the pickup location, farmers market or farmer-managed delivery option chosen.
- **DATA-4** Opens of pickup location and market previews, on the map and in lists, are counted in aggregate by location, tied to no individual.

## Data privacy

- **DPRIV-1** Search events store no IP address, device identifier or precise location, only the selected community. Time is stored to the day. Search text is kept short, and anything resembling a phone number, email or street address is stripped before storage.
- **DPRIV-2** Raw search events are reduced to aggregate counts and deleted after a configurable period. Buyer contact details are deleted a configurable period after the inquiry closes, leaving product type, community, status and outcome.
- **DPRIV-3** Community-level figures are not displayed when they rest on fewer than a configurable minimum of farms, searches or inquiries. The dashboard shows "not enough data". This applies to every analytics view, including outcomes and SNAP/EBT counts.
- **DPRIV-4** Raw search events and individual inquiries are visible only to administrators.

## Pilot metrics (Section 4, shown in the administrator dashboard)

- **METRIC-1** Inquiries sent; answered and how quickly; closed without a response.
- **METRIC-2** Farmer-reported outcomes, labelled self-reported.
- **METRIC-3** Listings confirmed in the last 14 days. Active farmers by community.
- **METRIC-4** Farmers reporting SNAP/EBT acceptance, labelled self-reported.
- **METRIC-5** Most-inquired products by community. Searches with no results. Most-chosen pickup locations and farmers markets.
- **METRIC-6** Wherever counts appear, the page states they reflect only people who used Musoko and that early pilot numbers are small.

## Claims wording (Section 2)

- **CLAIM-1** Nothing implies every farmer accepts SNAP/EBT, that a product qualifies for a health or nutrition benefit, or that prices are guaranteed affordable.
- **CLAIM-2** Meat, poultry, dairy and egg listings show the farmer's licence confirmation as "farmer-reported". Musoko does not verify it.

## Accessibility and performance

- **A11Y-1** Keyboard navigable, sufficient contrast, labelled form fields, alt text on images.
- **A11Y-2** The product list, not the map, is the default on phones. The map loads only when the user opens it.
- **A11Y-3** Images are compressed and lazy-loaded. Initial mobile page load is under roughly 1 MB.
- **A11Y-4** Plain language, large touch targets, and no step that requires typing when a choice will do.

## Seed data (Section 10)

- **SEED-1** About 12 farms across Helena-West Helena, Pine Bluff, Forrest City and surrounding Delta communities. Invented names that match no real business.
- **SEED-2** About 40 products across all eight categories, covering all three statuses, with varied prices, units and seasons.
- **SEED-3** Same product type in different unit sizes across farms, plus a few listings where no conversion is possible.
- **SEED-4** Mostly farmer-reported claims, with two or three verified.
- **SEED-5** Sample search events, some with no results.
- **SEED-6** Some listings with quantity and some without, including one "Available now" with a small quantity.
- **SEED-7** One administrator-created draft awaiting consent, and one published profile marked "awaiting farmer review".
- **SEED-8** At least one community with too little data, so "not enough data" is visible.
- **SEED-9** 5 farmers markets and 3 public pickup locations.
- **SEED-10** A mix of privacy settings: some exact locations, most not; some public contact details, most not.
- **SEED-11** A few farms with farmer-reported SNAP/EBT, most without.
- **SEED-12** Inquiries in all three statuses, including one closed without a response and some with outcomes.
- **SEED-13** One farmer, one buyer and one administrator demo account.

# README.md

# Musoko

Local food marketplace for the Arkansas Delta. Buyers find small farmers and contact them directly. An initiative of ReMix Ideas. Tagline: "Connecting Local Farmers and Communities."

Musoko is a discovery and inquiry tool. It is **not** a shop: no cart, no checkout, no payments, no delivery promises.

## Run it

Requires Node 20+ and pnpm 11 (or `corepack enable`).

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm dev
```

The app starts at [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). It runs with no `.env` file and no external credentials: demo mode is the default. Every page carries a demo watermark and a demo strip. Every seeded farm, product and market shows a "Demo" mark.

The demo strip has a role switcher (buyer, farmer, administrator) and a "Reset demo data" button. All changes (profile edits, listings, confirmations, registrations, inquiries, replies, outcomes, administrator actions) persist in `localStorage` under `musoko.demo.v1`, survive navigation, role switching and reload, and are wiped by "Reset demo data".

## Commands

```bash
pnpm dev            # run in demo mode
pnpm build          # production build
pnpm start          # serve the production build
pnpm typecheck      # tsc --noEmit
pnpm lint           # eslint, includes the import-boundary rules
pnpm test           # vitest, domain and data layers
pnpm test:e2e       # playwright, acceptance flows (one spec per acceptance group)
pnpm format         # prettier
```

The first `pnpm test:e2e` run needs the Playwright browser once:

```bash
pnpm exec playwright install chromium
```

A step is not finished until typecheck, lint, test and build all pass and the app runs.

| [docs/brief/Musoko-Development-Prompt-v5.pdf](docs/brief/Musoko-Development-Prompt-v5.pdf) | The client brief. Sections 1 to 3 are the contract. |

## How code is organised

Dependencies point one way:

```
app  →  features  →  domain
                  →  data/ports
                  →  design-system
data/adapters     →  data/ports, domain
```

- `domain/` is pure TypeScript. No React, no Next, no storage, no `Date.now()` — it takes `now` as an argument.
- `features/` never import from `data/adapters/`. They call through `data/ports/`.
- `design-system/` knows nothing about farms, products or inquiries.
- One feature does not import another feature's internals.
- ESLint (`no-restricted-imports` per folder) fails the build on a violation.

The data switch is one environment variable (`NEXT_PUBLIC_DATA_MODE`, default `demo`), read once in `src/config/env.ts` and used in `src/data/index.ts` to pick the demo adapter or the Supabase adapter.

## Environment variables

See [`.env.example`](.env.example). All are optional in demo mode.

| Variable | Scope | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_DATA_MODE` | client | `demo` (default) or `live`. Empty or absent means `demo`. |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` | client | Supabase project URL. Required when `NEXT_PUBLIC_DATA_MODE=live`. |
| `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` | client | Supabase anon key. Required when `NEXT_PUBLIC_DATA_MODE=live`. Protected by row-level security. |
| `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` | **server only** | Server actions and scheduled jobs. Never prefix with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. Never import into client code. |

No secrets reach the browser. Only `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` values are inlined, and none of them is a secret.

## What remains to configure for production

Demo mode is finished. Flipping `NEXT_PUBLIC_DATA_MODE` to `live` turns the Supabase adapter on, but a production launch still needs the following to be set up and signed off. Each line is work that is outside the code the agents built.

### Supabase (database, auth, storage)

- Create the Supabase project.
- Apply the migrations in `supabase/migrations/` (Postgres with PostGIS enabled).
- Load the seed, or an empty start: `supabase/seed.sql` is generated from `src/data/seed` and is suitable for staging only.
- Review row-level security on every table. The brief's privacy rule is that exact coordinates, street addresses, and farmer phone and email live in separate private tables (`farm_private_locations`, `farmer_private_contacts`, `inquiry_buyer_contacts`); these tables must be unreachable by the `anon` key, and readable only by the owning farmer, the writing buyer, and administrators.
- Decide the Storage bucket for farm and product photos; set its CORS and public-read policy.
- Set `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` and `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` in the production environment.

### SMS and email provider (required)

Musoko sends two notifications: inquiry notifications to farmers, and reply notifications (and auto-close notices) to buyers. In demo mode these go to the console and the in-app "demo outbox". In production:

- **SMS provider must be configured.** Twilio, Vonage, MessageBird or similar. The buyer's chosen reply method ("text" or "email") is stored with the inquiry; text replies require a working SMS provider. Add its credentials as server-side environment variables and wire them into the notification service in `src/data/adapters/supabase/`.
- Email provider (Resend, Postmark, SES or similar) for the email reply method and for buyer confirmations with the private status-page link.
- Decide the sending phone number (short code or long code, A2P 10DLC registered), the sender domain, SPF / DKIM / DMARC records and the "from" address that matches Musoko's identity.

### Map tiles

Demo mode uses the free OpenFreeMap style with no token. For production decide whether to stay on OpenFreeMap (check its rate limits for the expected audience), move to a paid tile source (MapTiler, Stadia, Protomaps self-hosted), or self-host. Set the tile source in the `MapConfig` port.

### Scheduled jobs

The lifecycle rules (availability lapse, inquiry reminder at 48 hours, auto-close at 14 days, search-event retention, buyer-contact retention) are one pure function in `src/domain/jobs`. Demo mode runs it on app load. In production it must be run on a schedule, as a Supabase scheduled function or a cron-triggered Next route handler, at least daily.

### Settings the project owner still has to decide

Default values are in `src/config/settings.ts`. Confirm each before launch:

- Availability confirmation window (default 14 days).
- Inquiry reminder delay (default 48 hours).
- Inquiry auto-close delay (default 14 days).
- Search-event retention period.
- Buyer-contact retention period after an inquiry closes.
- Minimum sample size for community-level figures ("not enough data" threshold).
- Accepted forms of administrator-recorded consent (in person, by phone, signed form) and the paper trail.

### Observability and operations

- Error reporting (Sentry or similar), with PII scrubbed.
- Logging retention for the scheduled jobs' output.
- A backup and restore policy for the Postgres database and the Storage bucket.
- An administrator account seeded in production and a documented way to add more.

### Review before launch

- Run `acceptance-check` against the live environment and keep the report.
- Re-check the privacy rules in the brief, Section 2: no "Verified farmer" badge; farmer contact and exact location are opt-in; the public API cannot return a private field; the demo watermark and demo strip are hidden in live mode; the "coming soon" note about Phase 2 and 3 features is the only mention of them.
- Confirm initial mobile page load is still under roughly 1 MB.
